title: The Lion’s Heir and the Donkey’s Speech
intro: The birth of the lion’s first cub brings a truce. Birds and beasts crowd into the courtyard, and each courtier must find something worthy to say. Shawqi gives the drinking songs to the monkey and the formal verse to the fox. Before the gathering breaks up, one of them will have to improvise a funeral speech.

translation: When the father of cubs sent out his herald
with glad news of his firstborn,
1.sharh: The lion is first named through his cubs. A herald takes what might have been family news and turns it into an occasion of state.

translation: the hunters of earth and sky came running,
and the court assembled to give its good wishes.
2.sharh: Ground predators and birds of prey share a single invitation. The two realms give a sense of the size of the gathering in the cub’s honour.

translation: A decree of safe conduct went out
through the land, to far and near.
3.sharh: Royal protection extends as far as the invitation. It makes the crowd of ordinarily incompatible guests possible.

translation: Tails thronged the courtyard till it could hold no more,
furred creatures and creatures with beaks.
4.sharh: The storyteller lets us see tails before we can make out their owners. Fur and beaks are enough to pick out two sorts of guest in a crush.

translation: Once the whole assembly was there,
the lion’s crier called among the royal train,
5.sharh: The herald has waited for a full house. “Assembly” and “royal train” lend a precise ceremonial order to the gathering of tails.

translation: “Is there a practised speaker here
to wish the prince long life?”
6.sharh: The assignment sounds harmless enough. The very words “long life” will be painful to remember when the speeches are over.

translation: The elephant, the high field marshal, rose
and spoke as the occasion required.
7.sharh: The highest-ranking speaker goes first. His performance is so perfectly conventional that the narrator can leave out every word.

translation: The fox, the envoy, followed with a recitation
till someone said, “A second Jarir.”
8.sharh: Jarir sets a high standard for praise and verbal combat. Calling the fox another Jarir is as much a part of the ceremony as the poem itself.

translation: The monkey who passed the winecup launched in.
“Well done, Abu Nuwas,” they cried.
9.sharh: The monkey’s job determines his poetic double. Abu Nuwas made wine a subject of poetry, and this would-be poet already has the cup in hand.

translation: The donkey signalled he would raise his voice,
intent on bringing honour to his kin.
10.sharh: The donkey sees the applause won by the first two speakers. The donkey sees a chance to distinguish his whole family, which makes the nature of his invocation especially telling.

translation: “In the name of him who made the barley,” he began,
“and sent the stick to donkeys.”
11.sharh: His ceremonial invocation takes in the two powers of a working donkey’s life, its feed and the stick. At last the reader hears a speaker’s actual words.

translation: The noise so shook the heir to the throne
that he died trembling in his cradle.
12.sharh: The prince who was to live so long has never left the cradle. In Arabic the words for succession and cradle end almost alike.

translation: The company fell upon the donkey
with every fang and claw they had.
13.sharh: The creatures’ bodies reappear, now as weapons. “Every” recalls the assembly’s full attendance at what began as a celebration.

translation: The fox was called upon for the funeral speech.
He found a way to have a dig at the poor beast.
14.sharh: The fox has found a second use for his eloquence. The donkey disappears under the crowd, and the funeral speech confirms what has become of him.

translation: “May God grant him no resting place.
A donkey he lived, and a donkey he died.”
15.sharh: The blessing expected at a funeral comes out as a curse. “Donkey” begins as a plain description of the animal and ends as the speaker’s verdict on his intelligence.

1.1.3.meaning: Herald, the officer who carries the ruler’s summons.

1.1.4-5.head: أَبو الأَشبال
1.1.4-5.meaning: “Father of cubs”, a name for the lion made newly apt by the birth.

1.2.1.head: بَشَّرَ
1.2.1.meaning: Brought glad tidings, here the official announcement of an heir.

2.1.2.head: سِباع
2.1.2.meaning: Predators. Extending the expression to the sky brings in the birds of prey.

2.2.3.head: الهَناء
2.2.3.meaning: Congratulations on a happy event, here the prince’s birth.

3.1.2.head: المَرسوم
3.1.2.meaning: A decree issued in the ruler’s name.

3.1.3.head: الأَمان
3.1.3.meaning: Safe conduct, a pledge that the guests may travel and attend in safety.

3.2.3.head: القاصي
3.2.3.meaning: The distant subject, paired with the one close at hand.

4.1.2.head: الذُّيول
4.1.2.meaning: Tails, the one conspicuous part standing for their jostling owners.

4.1.3-4.head: صَحن الدّار
4.1.3-4.meaning: “The house’s open space”, its inner courtyard.

5.1.4.head: الجَمعِيَّة
5.1.4.meaning: The assembled company. Once the guests are all present, the court can call for speeches.

5.2.5.head: المَعِيَّة
5.2.5.meaning: The royal entourage, those attending the king in person. A court office in nineteenth-century Egypt bore the same word in its name.

6.1.4.head: مُحسِن
6.1.4.meaning: Accomplished at a craft, in this case public speaking.

7.1.3.head: المُشير
7.1.3.meaning: Field marshal, a senior military rank given to the elephant.

7.1.4.meaning: Exalted in rank. The word suits both the marshal’s high office and the elephant towering over the assembly.

8.2.1.head: أَنشَدَ
8.2.1.meaning: Recited verse aloud before an audience.

8.2.5.head: جَرير
8.2.5.meaning: Jarir ibn Atiyya, an Umayyad poet known for praise and for his exchanges of invective with al-Farazdaq.

9.1.3-4.head: مُدير الكاس
9.1.3-4.meaning: “The one who sends the cup round”, the gathering’s cupbearer.

9.2.3-4.head: أَبو نُواس
9.2.3-4.meaning: Abu Nuwas, an Abbasid poet famous for poems of wine and drinking parties.

10.1.1.head: أَومَأَ
10.1.1.meaning: Signalled, here asking for the floor without speaking.

10.1.3.head: العَقيرَة
10.1.3.meaning: Voice, especially in the expression for lifting one’s voice in song or proclamation.

10.2.4.head: العَشيرَة
10.2.4.meaning: One’s clan or kindred, here all donkeykind.

11.2.1.head: باعِث
11.2.1.meaning: Sender. The stick wielded by a drover becomes part of the donkey’s solemn invocation.

12.1.3-4.head: وَلِيّ العَهد
12.1.3-4.meaning: Heir apparent, the cub for whose future reign the courtiers have assembled.

12.2.3.head: رِعدَة
12.2.3.meaning: Trembling, here the newborn cub’s convulsion of fright.

13.2.1.head: جُملَة
13.2.1.meaning: The sum of something. Every tooth and claw in the company bears down on one donkey.

14.1.3.head: التَّأبين
14.1.3.meaning: A funeral oration commemorating the dead.

14.2.3.head: التَّعريض
14.2.3.meaning: An insinuation, a way of getting in a jibe under cover of formal speech.

15.1.5.head: قَرار
15.1.5.meaning: Rest or repose, precisely what mourners normally wish the dead.

15.2.3.head: مَضى
15.2.3.meaning: Passed away, the funeral speaker’s word for dying. It answers “lived” at the beginning of the half.
